definition.text: The movement of dissolved contaminants with moving groundwater, studied by contaminant hydrogeology.

facts.text: Contaminants may be man-made, such as petroleum products, nitrate or radionuclides, or natural, such as arsenic or salinity.
They move by three main mechanisms: advection at seepage velocity, diffusion from high to low concentration, and hydrodynamic dispersion.
Aquifer properties beyond the flow itself affect how dissolved contaminants move.
Diffusion and dispersion only spread a contaminant, while retardation by adsorption slows its average velocity.
Polluted groundwater forms a plume whose advancing edge can reach wells and springs; its movement is analysed with hydrological transport or groundwater models.
Diffusion, adsorption, precipitation and decay all influence pollutant transport.

definition.text: The transport of a substance or quantity by the bulk motion of a fluid.

facts.text: It needs currents in a fluid, so it cannot happen in rigid solids, and it excludes transport by molecular diffusion.
Ink dumped in a river moves downstream as a pulse by advection while also spreading by diffusion; the sum of the two is convection.
In groundwater, advection carries contaminants along the main direction of flow at the seepage velocity.
The advection equation is a first-order hyperbolic partial differential equation derived from the conservation law of the transported quantity.

definition.text: The spreading of dissolved contaminants away from the mean path of the groundwater carrying them, caused by small-scale heterogeneity and uneven velocities in the porous medium.

facts.text: Its strength is expressed by empirical dispersivities: longitudinal (αL) for solute ahead of or behind the mean flow, transverse (αT) for solute to the sides.
At the microscopic scale, water passing each soil particle must go left, right, up or down, so solute spreads around the mean path.
Over long distances, zones of higher and lower permeability give preferential paths that spread contaminants irregularly.
Dispersivity reflects details averaged away in a macroscopic model, such as thin gravel or clay beds in sand, so it is partly a measure of missing information.
It is therefore often claimed to depend on scale: dispersivity through 1 m3 of aquifer differs from that through 1 cm3 of the same material.
Salinity models need dispersivity as a soil input alongside water retention and unsaturated hydraulic conductivity.

definition.text: The random thermal movement of molecules that carries solutes from high to low concentration.

facts.text: Time to diffuse grows with the square of distance, so diffusion matters over small distances but spreads solutes slowly over large ones.
Its coefficient is small and often negligible, except where groundwater flows extremely slowly, as in clay aquitards.
Diffusion is a physical process, whereas dispersion is an empirical factor written in the same mathematical form.

definition.text: The slowing of a contaminant's average movement relative to groundwater because it adsorbs to the soil, measured by a retardation factor.

facts.text: The factor is analogous to the retardation factor of chromatography.
Adsorption holds the contaminant back until the amount set by the adsorption equilibrium has been adsorbed.
Less soluble contaminants can move hundreds or thousands of times slower than water, so only the more soluble species travel far.
The factor depends on the chemistry of both the contaminant and the aquifer.
Unlike diffusion and dispersion, which merely spread a contaminant, retardation changes its global average velocity, so it can be much slower than the water.
In chromatography the retardation factor R is the fraction of the substance in the mobile phase at equilibrium: the quantity in the mobile phase divided by the total quantity in the system.
In planar chromatography RF is the substance's travel distance over the solvent front's, always between 0 and 1 because nothing outruns the solvent; 2.5 cm over 5.0 cm gives 0.50.

definition.text: A parabolic partial differential equation for a quantity moved by both diffusion and convection (advection).

facts.text: It is also called the advection–diffusion or scalar transport equation.
It follows from the continuity equation, with diffusive flux from Fick's first law, −D∇c, and advective flux vc.
A source or sink term R adds or removes the quantity, as when a chemical reaction creates or destroys a species.
For flow in porous media, the velocity in the equation is the superficial velocity.
Most soil water and solute models, such as SWAP, DrainMod-S, UnSatChem and Hydrus, couple the Richards equation with it to move salts by advection and dispersion.

definition.text: Transport in which colloidal particles carry contaminants through surface water and groundwater.

facts.text: Colloids also move through surface soils and the ground depending on soil structure, compaction and particle size; the process drew real attention only in the 1980s.
Radionuclides, heavy metals and organic pollutants sorb easily onto suspended colloids, which may be inorganic (clays, iron oxy-hydroxides) or organic (humic and fulvic substances).
Colloids are suspected in long-range plutonium transport at the Nevada Nuclear Test Site.
Inorganic colloids barely move in compacted bentonite and deep clay, which ultrafilter them.

definition.text: Computer models that simulate water flow and solute transport in unsaturated soil by solving the Richards equation numerically.

facts.text: Hydrus takes soil hydraulic parameters for the water retention and unsaturated conductivity functions, plus initial and boundary conditions.
Most such models, including SWAP, DrainMod-S, UnSatChem and Hydrus, join the Richards equation to a convection–diffusion equation for salts.
The one-dimensional HYDRUS1D program is available online and used to estimate groundwater recharge.

definition.text: A method of tracking flows by adding dye to a liquid as a tracer.

facts.text: It can be qualitative, showing a flow exists, or quantitative, measuring dye amounts with instruments such as fluorometers.
Fluorescein, first developed in 1871, and its sodium salt uranine remain among the best tracers, with rhodamine, pyranine and sulforhodamine B.
Organic matter, other chemicals, sunlight and acidic water affect dye performance.
Dye traces showed karst groundwater moving 0.8 to 11.3 km a day and that models assuming uniform porosity do not fit karst aquifers.

title: Breakthrough curve

definition.text: The course of a solute's concentration at the outlet of a column of porous material after a step change in inlet concentration.

facts.text: A fixed bed is purged with a carrier, then the adsorptive is added so that inlet concentration changes in a step, and the outlet concentration is monitored; chromatography instead uses pulses.
Integrating the area above the whole curve gives the material's maximum loading, and the time until the outlet reaches a threshold concentration gives its usable sorption capacity.
The curve's shape carries information on mass-transfer properties, which can be evaluated by fitting simplified models to the data.
The source page frames this in adsorption engineering; the soil-column version is not described in it.

notes: thin: page is about fixed-bed adsorbers, no soil-column or leaching sentences; a soil-column leaching source would fill it.

definition.text: A dimensionless number giving the ratio of advective to diffusive transport rate.

facts.text: For mass transfer, Pe = L u / D, with L a characteristic length, u flow velocity and D the diffusion coefficient; it equals the Reynolds number times the Schmidt number.
It can also be written as the ratio of diffusion time to advection time.
Where Pe is much greater than 1, advection predominates in mass transport because diffusion takes much longer.
